bio.text: I do dare to believe … that, like Horace … I have executed a work which will go down to posterity, and which will endure for as long as there are men desirous of knowing all that has survived until our day, of the ruins of the most famous city of the universe.

source.author: Giovanni Battista Piranesi
source.title: On his etchings of Rome
source.publisher: translated in Arthur M. Samuel, Piranesi (B. T. Batsford, 1910; Internet Archive scan)

bio.text: In 1740 Piranesi left Venice for Rome in the suite of the ambassador to the Papal Court, and was lodged for a time at the Venetian Embassy. He studied etching under Giuseppe Vasi, the engraver of one of the largest views of Rome

source.author: Arthur M. Hind
source.title: Giovanni Battista Piranesi: A Critical Study

bio.text: the sublime dreams of Piranesi, who seems to have conceived visions of Rome beyond what it boasted even in the meridian of its splendour. Savage as Salvator Rosa, fierce as Michael Angelo, and exuberant as Rubens, he has imagined scenes that would startle geometry, and exhaust the Indies to realize.
